core_summary: This chapter explores the magnetic fields generated by electric currents and moving charges, beginning with Oersted's discovery. It details magnetic field patterns around straight conductors, circular loops, and solenoids, utilizing the Right-Hand Thumb Rule. It explains the force experienced by current-carrying conductors in magnetic fields via Fleming's Left-Hand Rule and its application in electric motors. Finally, it outlines domestic wiring systems, color-coded insulation, grounding safety, and circuit protection against short-circuiting and overloading.
key_concepts: Oersted's discovery proving that electric currents produce surrounding magnetic fields
Magnetic Field Lines: Closed continuous loops emerging from North pole and entering South pole externally; density indicates magnetic field strength; lines never intersect
- Straight conductor: Concentric circles whose direction is determined by Right-Hand Thumb Rule
- Circular loop: Concentric arcs becoming straight lines at loop center; field strength proportional to number of turns (n)
- Solenoid: Uniform parallel straight field lines internally, mimicking a bar magnet; used to create electromagnets with soft iron cores
Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field (Ampere's principle): Maximum force occurs when current direction is perpendicular to magnetic field
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: Thumb (Force/Motion), Forefinger (Magnetic Field), Middle Finger (Current) mutually perpendicular
Electric Motor: Device converting electrical energy into mechanical energy using armature coil, permanent magnet, split-ring commutator, and carbon brushes
Electromagnetism in medical diagnostics: Weak biomagnetic fields in human heart and brain enabling Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

Domestic Electric Circuits: Live wire (red/brown, 220 V), Neutral wire (black/blue, 0 V), Earth wire (green/yellow, ground protection); 15 A rating for high-power appliances and 5 A rating for bulbs/fans
Circuit Hazards & Safety: Short-circuiting (direct live-neutral contact), Overloading (excessive appliance draw), Fuse protection, and Earthing metallic bodies

key_terms.definition: The region surrounding a magnet or current-carrying conductor in which magnetic forces can be detected.
Imaginary continuous curved lines representing the direction and relative strength of a magnetic field.
Rule stating that if a straight current-carrying conductor is held in the right hand with thumb pointing along current, wrapped fingers show magnetic field line direction.
A long cylindrical coil consisting of many closely wrapped turns of insulated copper wire.
A temporary magnet produced by placing a soft iron core inside a current-carrying solenoid coil.
Rule determining direction of magnetic force on a conductor: stretch thumb, forefinger, and middle finger perpendicular—forefinger=field, middle finger=current, thumb=motion/force.
The soft iron core wrapped with copper coil that rotates inside the magnetic field of an electric motor or generator.
A split-ring copper device in a DC motor that reverses current direction through the armature coil every half rotation to maintain continuous rotation.
The supply wire carrying current at high potential (220 V relative to earth in India), covered with red/brown insulation.
The return wire completing domestic circuits at zero potential relative to earth, covered with black/blue insulation.
Safety conductor with green/yellow insulation connected to a metal ground plate, preventing electric shocks from appliance metallic bodies.
Hazardous condition when live and neutral wires make direct contact, causing current to spike abruptly.
Condition where total current drawn by connected appliances exceeds the safe carrying capacity of circuit wires.

key_takeaways: Magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops and never intersect because a compass cannot point in two directions simultaneously at one point.
The magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid is completely uniform, represented by parallel straight field lines.
Split-ring commutators in electric motors reverse coil current direction every half-turn, ensuring unidirectional continuous mechanical rotation.
Earthing protects human users by diverting any leaking electrical current safely into the ground through a low-resistance path.
Domestic appliances are connected in parallel across live and neutral wires so each operates under a uniform 220 V potential difference.
